title: DKIM
summary: DomainKeys Identified Mail, usually shortened to DKIM, is an email authentication method that lets a sending domain attach a cryptographic signature to a message so a receiving system can verify that the message really came from that domain and was not altered on the way. The signer hashes selected header fields and part of the body, then signs that hash with a private key. The matching public key is published as a TXT record in the domain's DNS under a selector name, so the receiver can fetch it and validate the signature. DKIM constrains integrity and domain accountability, not the honesty of the content: a phisher can sign their own mail with their own valid key. It also survives forwarding poorly, because a relay that modifies a subject line or adds a footer breaks the body hash unless the signer chose which fields to sign carefully. The mistake people usually make is assuming a passing DKIM check means the message is trustworthy, when it only proves which domain signed it and that the signed parts arrived unchanged.

beginner.definition: DKIM stands for DomainKeys Identified Mail. It adds a hidden digital signature to an email. The receiving mail server checks that signature. If it matches, the message really came from that domain and nobody changed it on the way.
beginner.whyItMatters: Anyone can type a famous company name into the sender field of an email. Without a check, your mail server cannot tell real mail from a fake. DKIM gives a proof that travels with the message. It protects your customers from forged mail that pretends to be you. It also helps your own honest mail reach the inbox instead of the spam folder.
howItWorks: Your mail system creates a pair of keys: a private key you keep, and a public key you share.
You publish the public key in a DNS record that anyone can look up.
When you send a message, your server calculates a fingerprint of chosen parts of it.
The server signs that fingerprint with the private key and adds the result as a header.
The receiving server looks up your public key and checks that the signature is valid.
If the check passes, the receiver knows the signed parts were not changed.
beginner.example: Think of a wax seal on an old letter. The sender presses a unique stamp into hot wax, and the family crest is known to everyone. A reader who sees an unbroken seal knows the letter came from that house and nobody opened it. But a good seal only proves who sent the letter. It says nothing about whether the news inside is true.
takeaways: DKIM proves which domain signed a message and that signed parts were not changed.
A valid signature does not mean the message is safe or honest.
Forwarding can break a signature, so keep the signed fields simple and stable.

objectives: Explain what DKIM is and which two properties of an email it actually verifies.
Describe how a key pair and a published DNS record work together to validate a message.
Recognise the difference between proving a sender's identity and proving a message is safe.
Identify why forwarding and mailing lists can cause a valid signature to fail.
Explain how DKIM supports the wider email authentication picture alongside related standards.
